countries.name: England
countries.description: The initial Music Atlas country context: a place where music scenes, artists, and albums are connected through meaningful historical, cultural, geographical, or artistic relationships.

genres.name: Merseybeat
genres.description: A bright early-1960s guitar-pop style associated with Liverpool beat groups and the city's club culture.

genres.name: Punk rock
genres.description: A direct, fast, and confrontational style that became central to London's late-1970s youth culture and independent music networks.

genres.name: Heavy metal
genres.description: A heavy rock style whose early development is strongly connected to Birmingham, Black Sabbath, and the English industrial landscape.

genres.name: Post-punk
genres.description: An exploratory field that extended punk's energy into darker textures, experimentation, electronic sounds, and new forms of songwriting.

genres.name: Synth-pop
genres.description: Electronic pop built around synthesizers, programmed rhythms, and accessible song forms, with a major English chapter in Sheffield.

genres.name: Shoegaze
genres.description: A guitar-based style marked by dense effects, blended vocals, and immersive textures, strongly represented by English bands of the late 1980s and early 1990s.

genres.name: Trip hop
genres.description: A spacious fusion of hip-hop, dub, soul, and electronic production closely associated with Bristol's 1990s musical culture.

genres.name: Grime
genres.description: A stark, rhythmically urgent style shaped by MCing, electronic production, pirate radio, and East London's early-2000s networks.

genres.name: UK garage
genres.description: A club-oriented British dance style whose London scenes, rhythms, and radio networks form important context for grime.

genres.name: Dubstep
genres.description: A bass-focused electronic style included here for its meaningful London connections and its relationship to UK garage's aftermath.

scenes.name: Liverpool Merseybeat Scene
scenes.description: A Liverpool club and beat-group culture centred on venues such as the Cavern Club and active in the early 1960s.

scenes.name: London Punk Scene
scenes.description: A late-1970s London network of venues, bands, fashion, media, and audiences that made punk a visible cultural force.

scenes.name: Birmingham Heavy Metal Scene
scenes.description: A Birmingham and West Midlands context for heavy metal's early development, industrial identity, and working musicians.

scenes.name: Manchester Post-Punk / Factory Context
scenes.description: A Manchester context around post-punk, Factory Records, Joy Division, and the city's post-industrial cultural transformation.

scenes.name: Sheffield Electronic / Synth-Pop Scene
scenes.description: A Sheffield network linking experimental electronics, industrial textures, and synth-pop's movement into accessible forms.

scenes.name: Bristol Sound / Trip Hop Scene
scenes.description: A Bristol creative context shaped by sound-system culture, dub, hip-hop, electronic production, and artists associated with the Bristol Sound.

scenes.name: East London Grime Scene
scenes.description: An early-2000s and ongoing East London network of pirate radio, crews, MCs, audiences, and independent circulation around grime.

artists.name: The Beatles
artists.description: The Liverpool group provides a foundational route into Merseybeat, Cavern-era culture, and early-1960s English pop history.

artists.name: Gerry and the Pacemakers
artists.description: A central Liverpool beat group that shows the Merseybeat story was broader than a single band.

artists.name: Black Sabbath
artists.description: The Birmingham band is a key route into heavy metal and England's role in the genre's early development.

artists.name: Judas Priest
artists.description: Judas Priest represents a later consolidation of English heavy metal beyond its earliest Birmingham landmarks.

artists.name: Sex Pistols
artists.description: The Sex Pistols offer a direct entry into London's first-wave punk sound, attitude, and cultural impact.

artists.name: The Clash
artists.description: The Clash connect London punk to reggae, ska, rockabilly, and broader urban commentary.

artists.name: Joy Division
artists.description: Joy Division is a key artist for understanding Manchester post-punk, Factory Records, and the city's changing cultural landscape.

artists.name: New Order
artists.description: New Order demonstrates continuity from Manchester post-punk into electronic and dance-oriented music.

artists.name: The Human League
artists.description: The Human League provides an accessible route into Sheffield's electronic history and synth-pop's movement into mainstream pop.

artists.name: Cabaret Voltaire
artists.description: Cabaret Voltaire represents Sheffield's experimental electronic roots and the textures behind later synth-pop visibility.

artists.name: Ride
artists.description: Ride offers a strong Oxford entry into English shoegaze and the dense guitar sound of the early 1990s.

artists.name: Slowdive
artists.description: Slowdive adds a Reading perspective on shoegaze and its overlap with dream-pop textures.

artists.name: Massive Attack
artists.description: Massive Attack provides a central route into Bristol's fusion of dub, hip-hop, soul, and electronic production.

artists.name: Portishead
artists.description: Portishead offers an accessible and cinematic route into Bristol trip hop and its distinctive local culture.

artists.name: Tricky
artists.description: Tricky represents a more fractured and personal Bristol path connected to the city's wider sound-system and production culture.

artists.name: Dizzee Rascal
artists.description: Dizzee Rascal provides a clear East London gateway into early grime and its relationship with pirate radio and MC culture.

artists.name: Wiley
artists.description: Wiley helps explain early grime, its East London networks, and debates around the language used to describe its sound.

artists.name: Burial
artists.description: Burial provides a London-rooted electronic entry connected to the aftermath of UK garage and dubstep without requiring a specific Scene association.

albums.title: Please Please Me
albums.description: This debut album is an accessible entry into The Beatles, Liverpool's Merseybeat culture, and early-1960s English pop history.

albums.title: How Do You Like It?
albums.description: Gerry and the Pacemakers' debut helps show the Liverpool scene was a wider musical community rather than a story about one group.

albums.title: Paranoid
albums.description: Paranoid is a defining heavy metal entry and a direct route into Birmingham's role in the genre's development.

albums.title: British Steel
albums.description: British Steel represents the later consolidation of English heavy metal and extends the story beyond Black Sabbath's first moment.

albums.title: Never Mind the Bollocks, Here's the Sex Pistols
albums.description: This album offers a direct route into London's punk sound, attitude, and late-1970s cultural impact.

albums.title: London Calling
albums.description: London Calling shows how a scene-central punk band expanded into reggae, ska, rockabilly, and wider urban commentary.

albums.title: Unknown Pleasures
albums.description: Unknown Pleasures is a core post-punk album and a key entry into Manchester's Factory context.

albums.title: Power, Corruption & Lies
albums.description: This New Order album demonstrates continuity from Manchester post-punk into electronic and dance-oriented music.

albums.title: Dare
albums.description: Dare is an accessible synth-pop entry and a key album for Sheffield electronic music reaching a broad audience.

albums.title: Mix-Up
albums.description: Mix-Up represents Sheffield's experimental electronic roots and the darker textures around its synth-pop story.

albums.title: Nowhere
albums.description: Nowhere is a strong Oxford entry into English shoegaze and the immersive guitar sound of the early 1990s.

albums.title: Souvlaki
albums.description: Souvlaki adds a Reading perspective on shoegaze and its overlap with dream-pop textures.

albums.title: Blue Lines
albums.description: Blue Lines is a central Bristol Sound entry, bridging dub, hip-hop, soul, and electronic production.

albums.title: Dummy
albums.description: Dummy offers an accessible and historically significant route into Bristol trip hop's darker, cinematic side.

albums.title: Maxinquaye
albums.description: Maxinquaye represents a personal and fractured Bristol path connected to the city's wider production culture.

albums.title: Boy in da Corner
albums.description: Boy in da Corner is an essential early grime album and a clear East London discovery point.

albums.title: Treddin' on Thin Ice
albums.description: This album helps represent early grime, East London's networks, and debates around grime and eski-beat terminology.

albums.title: Untrue
albums.description: Untrue provides a London-rooted electronic entry connected to the aftermath of UK garage and dubstep without forcing a Scene association.
